svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Google Cloud IAM and the Workspace or Cloud Identity admin plane are two separate control planes, why IAM deny policies reach only some permissions and none in the directory plane, why the Organization Administrator role is narrower than it looks in only one direction, and what the super admin guidance actually prescribes
svg.title: Organization roles and the super admin problem: two control planes, one of them outside IAM
svg.text: The most powerful account is not governed by the system this series has been about.
Deny policies are the only thing that overrides an allow, and they do not reach the directory plane at all.
Two control planes, and the super admin lives in the one IAM does not govern
Plane
Governs
Controlled by
Google Cloud IAM
org, folders, projects, resources
allow + deny + org policies
Workspace / Cloud Identity
users, groups, domains, SSO, 2SV
Workspace admin roles
A super admin has administrative capabilities that include Cloud Identity. Org Admin is an IAM role.
Deny is the only override, and it does not reach everything
IAM always checks relevant deny policies before checking relevant allow policies.
But: you can use SOME, BUT NOT ALL IAM permissions in deny policies.
My count of the supported-permissions page, 7 Oct 2026: 10,581 identifiers across 179 services,
and ZERO under cloudidentity or admin.googleapis. The directory plane is not in the list.
And Organization Administrator is narrower than it looks in one direction only
Its own description: access to manage IAM policies and view organization policies.
No compute, no storage, no data. But it holds setIamPolicy on the organization.
Which is total authority one step removed: it can grant itself anything else.
What the guidance actually prescribes
Separate accounts, and keep the super admin OUT of the Organization Administrator group.
A physical security key for the initial account, kept in a safe place at your physical location.
Self-recovery is disabled by default for new customers. Keep it disabled.
Alert on SetIamPolicy(). Mirror your suspension policy into the third-party IdP.
That last alert fires on #48 Service Agent Manager too: Google writes to your policy as well.
Deny has exceptionPrincipals by design, so a break-glass account is an exemption you author.
#54 elevation that expires. #55 the account that cannot be elevated because it never descends:
its power is in another plane, and the best controls on offer are a key in a safe and an alert.
